title: The Open Digital Library: Why We Built BitLibrary and What It Means for You
description: The story behind BitLibrary — why open access to books, curriculum, and research matters, and how one platform is trying to make knowledge truly free for everyone.
content:
I remember walking into the Tribhuvan University library in Kathmandu for the first time. It was packed — students everywhere, sharing worn-out textbooks, copying notes by hand because there weren't enough copies to go around. One book for every twenty students. That scene stayed with me.

A few years later, I was browsing Project Gutenberg and it hit me: those 70,000 free books could fill an entire university library ten times over. But none of those students in that crowded room knew they existed. The books were open. The access wasn't.

That gap — between knowledge that *is* free and knowledge that *feels* free — is exactly what BitLibrary tries to close.

## The Problem with Free

Here is the truth about free books online: they are scattered across a hundred different websites, each with its own search, its own design, its own idea of what a book looks like. Gutendex has the classics. Open Library has the rare ones. Internet Archive has the scans. Google Books has the previews. arXiv has the research papers. LibriVox has the audio. None of them talk to each other.

If you are a student in Nepal trying to find your Class 10 science textbook, an audio version of a Nepali poem, and a research paper on quantum computing — you would need to visit four different websites, learn four different interfaces, and pray that the one you need actually works on your phone.

That is not open. That is just fragmented.

## What an Open Digital Library Actually Means

When we say open digital library, we are not just talking about free books. We are talking about a different philosophy entirely.

| Traditional Digital Library | Open Digital Library |
|---------------------------|-------------------|
| You go to the books | The books come to you |
| One source, one catalog | Every source, unified |
| Read only what they have | Read anything you can find |
| Search within their walls | Search across all walls |
| You adapt to their interface | The interface adapts to you |

The difference is subtle but crucial. A traditional digital library is a walled garden, even if the entrance is free. An open digital library is a city with no gates — you can walk in from any direction, and every path leads somewhere useful.

## Why BitLibrary Exists

BitLibrary started with a simple observation: the infrastructure for universal access already exists. The books are digitized. The catalogues are built. The audio is recorded. What was missing was someone to connect the dots.

We built BitLibrary to:

1. **Unify** — Search across Project Gutenberg, Open Library, Internet Archive, Google Books, arXiv, LibriVox, and others from one place
2. **Simplify** — Read books, listen to audiobooks, browse curriculum, and search research databases without switching apps
3. **Localize** — Focus on Nepal's educational needs first, with CDC curriculum textbooks and Nepali content
4. **Free** — No subscriptions, no logins, no paywalls

## What Makes This Different

Most digital library projects start with a collection. They say: here are our books, come read them. BitLibrary starts with a question: what do you need, and where can we find it?

| Approach | Most Digital Libraries | BitLibrary |
|----------|----------------------|------------|
| Focus | Building a collection | Finding what exists |
| Content | What they own or license | What is openly available |
| Scope | One catalog | Multiple sources unified |
| User | Generalized | Nepal-focused first |

This does not mean BitLibrary replaces Project Gutenberg or Open Library. It means BitLibrary stands on their shoulders. They built the libraries. We built the door.

> "Libraries store the energy that fuels the imagination. They open up windows to the world and inspire us to explore and achieve, and contribute to improving our quality of life."

## What Comes Next

The library is never finished. There are always more sources to connect, more formats to support, more communities to serve. Right now we are focused on making the existing content easier to find and use. Down the road, the same infrastructure can support community annotations, reading groups, shared curricula, and tools that let teachers and students build their own libraries out of the public domain.

But none of that matters if the door is locked. So we are starting with the door. Everything on BitLibrary is free, always, no account required.

The books are already there. They have been waiting. We just need to help people find them.

## Understanding Copyright Expiration

Books enter the **public domain** when their copyright expires. The rules vary by country, but the basic principle is that after a certain period, creative works belong to everyone.

## Copyright Terms by Country

| Country | General Rule | Duration |
|---------|-------------|----------|
| **United States** | Life + 70 years for works after 1978 | Varies for older works |
| **United Kingdom** | Life + 70 years | Same for most countries |
| **Canada** | Life + 50 years (Life + 70 after extension) | Transitioning |
| **Nepal** | Life + 50 years | As per Copyright Act 2059 |
| **India** | Life + 60 years | Section 22 of Copyright Act |
| **European Union** | Life + 70 years | Harmonized across EU |

## How to Calculate Public Domain Status

A book is generally in the public domain if:

- The **author died more than 70 years ago** (in most countries)
- It was **published before 1928** (in the US, as of 2026)
- It was **published without copyright notice** before certain dates
- The **copyright was not renewed** (for older US works)

### Examples for 2026

| Author | Died | Status |
|--------|------|--------|
| Jane Austen | 1817 | Public domain worldwide |
| Charles Dickens | 1870 | Public domain worldwide |
| Leo Tolstoy | 1910 | Public domain worldwide |
| Virginia Woolf | 1941 | PD in Life+50 countries |
| George Orwell | 1950 | Copyrighted in Life+70 countries |

## What Entered the Public Domain in 2026

In the United States, works published in **1930** enter the public domain in 2026. This includes books like The Maltese Falcon by Dashiell Hammett and Cimarron by Edna Ferber, as well as various films and musical works from 1930.

## Why Copyright Expiration Matters

- **Preservation** — Libraries can digitize and preserve old works
- **Education** — Free access to foundational texts
- **Creativity** — Authors can adapt and build upon old works
- **Accessibility** — Anyone can read, regardless of income

> Public domain is not a loophole — it is a feature of copyright law designed to foster culture and knowledge.

title: How I Found a Free Library of 70,000 Books

content:
I found Project Gutenberg by accident. I was looking for a free copy of a Jane Austen novel I had never read, and a friend told me about this site where volunteers typed up old books and gave them away. I thought it was a scam. Who gives away books for free?

The answer is: about 70,000 people, over five decades.

Public domain books are works whose copyright has expired. In most countries, copyright lasts for the author's life plus 70 years. After that, the book belongs to everyone. You can read it, download it, print it, share it, even turn it into a movie if you want. Nobody owns it anymore.

This is an enormous pool of material. Almost every classic you heard about in school is in the public domain. Pride and Prejudice, Moby Dick, Great Expectations, Frankenstein, Dracula, Alice in Wonderland, The Republic, On the Origin of Species. All free. All legal.

## Where the Books Come From

The biggest source is Project Gutenberg. It started in 1971 when Michael Hart typed the Declaration of Independence into a computer and sent it to everyone on the network. That was the first ebook. Today, thousands of volunteers have contributed to make the library what it is.

Other sources include Open Library, which has scanned copies of millions of books, and the Internet Archive, which preserves everything from 78 rpm records to old websites. Each source has its own focus. Project Gutenberg has clean text files. The Internet Archive has page scans that look like the original book.

## What You Can Actually Find

| Category | Examples |
|----------|----------|
| Novels | Austen, Dickens, Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Melville, Bronte |
| Science | Darwin, Newton, Galileo, Faraday, Curie |
| Philosophy | Plato, Aristotle, Nietzsche, Kant, Rousseau |
| Poetry | Whitman, Dickinson, Keats, Wordsworth, Yeats |
| Drama | Shakespeare, Ibsen, Chekhov, Shaw, Wilde |
| History | Gibbon, Herodotus, Thucydides, Macaulay |
| Children | Carroll, Baum, Barrie, Grahame, Alcott |

Not everything is there. Recent books, foreign language works, and obscure academic texts are often missing. But the core of Western literature is covered.

On BitLibrary, you do not need to visit multiple sites. Search once and results come from all these sources at once. Find a book, click it, start reading in your browser. No account, no payment, no ads.

The hardest part is choosing what to read first. I started with Austen and did not stop for a year.

title: Inside Nepal's School System: A Guide to the CDC Curriculum
description: What it is like to study in Nepal's public schools, how the CDC develops its textbooks, and where the system is heading next.
content:
I visited a public school in Sindhupalchok district a few years ago. The building had two rooms, a tin roof, and about sixty students spread across grades one through five. One teacher handled most of them. The textbooks on the desks were worn thin, passed down from older siblings, then cousins, then neighbors' children.

The teacher told me she had not received new textbooks in three years. The ones they had came from the Curriculum Development Centre, or CDC, which prints and distributes textbooks for every public school in Nepal.

This is the reality of the CDC curriculum. It is not just a list of subjects. It is the backbone of education for millions of children, many of whom have no other learning materials.

## How the CDC Works

The CDC, under the Ministry of Education, develops the national curriculum for grades one through twelve. It decides what subjects are taught, what each grade should cover, and what textbooks look like. Schools across the country follow this curriculum.

| Level | Grades | Age Range | Key Exams |
|-------|--------|-----------|-----------|
| Basic Education (Primary) | 1 to 5 | 5 to 10 | School level |
| Basic Education (Lower Secondary) | 6 to 8 | 11 to 13 | District exams |
| Secondary | 9 to 10 | 14 to 15 | SEE |
| Higher Secondary | 11 to 12 | 16 to 17 | NEB exams |

## Subjects Across the Grades

The core subjects stay consistent from grade one through ten: Nepali, English, Mathematics, Science, Social Studies, and Health. In grades one through three, there is also Hamro Serofero (Our Surroundings), which combines science and social studies into one subject.

In grades eleven and twelve, students choose a stream: Science, Management, Humanities, or Education. Each stream has its own set of specialized subjects.

## The Digital Gap

CDC textbooks are free for public school students in theory. In practice, distribution is uneven. Remote schools may receive their shipments months late, if at all. Digital access could close this gap, but reliable internet is still limited in many parts of the country.

BitLibrary hosts digital copies of CDC textbooks for all grades. Where internet is available, students and teachers can access them for free. The goal is not to replace printed books but to provide a backup when the printed ones do not arrive.

For a deeper look at specific grades, see the subject guides on this blog: class by class, subject by subject, with study tips for each level.

title: How to Get Started with LibriVox: A Practical Guide
description: Everything you need to know to start listening to free audiobooks on LibriVox. No sign up required, no hidden fees, no catch.
content:
The first time I opened the LibriVox website, I had no idea what I was looking at. The design is plain. The navigation takes some getting used to. There are no curated recommendations or personalized playlists. It looks like a website from 2005 because in many ways it is.

But behind that no-frills interface is a library of over 15,000 free audiobooks, all read by volunteers, all in the public domain, all completely free to download and listen to.

## What Is LibriVox?

LibriVox is a project that records public domain books into audiobooks. Volunteers around the world pick books they love, record themselves reading them, and submit the recordings. There is no editing team, no quality control beyond community standards, and no payment. The whole thing runs on enthusiasm.

This means quality varies. Some recordings are as polished as anything you would buy on Audible. Others sound like they were recorded in a closet with a laptop microphone. But the best ones have something that professional recordings rarely capture: genuine love for the book.

## How to Find Good Recordings

| What to Look For | Why |
|------------------|-----|
| Solo readings | One narrator for the whole book. More consistent. |
| High number of downloads | Other listeners vetted it for you. |
| Recent recordings | Better microphone quality. |
| Readers with many books | Experienced narrators tend to be better. |

## How to Start Listening on BitLibrary

1. Go to the Audiobooks section on BitLibrary.
2. Browse by category or search for a specific title.
3. Click any book to see its detail page.
4. Press Play. That is it.

Your progress is saved automatically. You can switch between devices and pick up where you left off. Playback speed is adjustable from 0.75x to 2x.

## What to Listen to First

If you have never listened to a LibriVox recording, start with a book you already know and love. The familiarity helps you get past the occasional background noise or narration quirk. Pride and Prejudice read by Elizabeth Klett is a good starting point. So is The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes read by David Clarke.

Once you get used to the style, branch out. The range of books is enormous, and new recordings are added every week. Everything is free, and nothing ever expires.

title: The Library in Your Pocket vs. The One Down the Street
description: I spend time in both digital and physical libraries. Here is what each one does better, where each falls short, and why you need both.
content:
I grew up going to the Kathmandu public library. It was a small building with creaky wooden floors and the smell of old paper. The librarian knew my name. She would save new arrivals for me behind the counter. I spent whole afternoons there, reading on the floor between shelves because there were not enough chairs.

These days I read mostly on my phone. The library in my pocket has hundreds of thousands of books. I can search the full text of any of them in seconds. I never have to worry about late fees or opening hours.

But I miss the smell. I miss the librarian knowing my name.

## What Digital Libraries Do Better

| Advantage | How It Works |
|-----------|-------------|
| Instant access | Open an app, find a book, start reading in under a minute. |
| No wait for popular books | Everyone can read the same book at the same time. |
| Full text search | Find any word or phrase across an entire book instantly. |
| No physical limits | Shelf space does not matter. Libraries can hold millions of books. |
| Always open | 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. No closing time. |
| Free delivery | No need to travel. The book comes to you. |

## What Physical Libraries Do Better

| Advantage | How It Works |
|-----------|-------------|
| Discovery | Browsing a shelf leads to books you would never search for. |
| Community | Storytime for kids, book clubs, study spaces, events. |
| Expertise | Librarians know their collections and can give real recommendations. |
| Focus | It is easier to concentrate on a physical book than a screen. |
| Access for everyone | Not everyone has a device or reliable internet. Libraries bridge that gap. |

digital libraries are unmatched for convenience and scale. Physical libraries are unmatched for serendipity and human connection. Neither replaces the other.

## The Hybrid Future

The best scenario is having access to both. BitLibrary tries to play its part by making digital books easy to find and read. But a good digital library points you toward physical libraries too. It tells you where to find a local branch, what events are happening, and which books are available on the shelf.

Physical libraries are not going away. They are changing, just like everything else. The ones that survive will be the ones that embrace digital tools while keeping what makes them special: the quiet, the community, and the feeling of walking out with a stack of books you did not know you needed.

title: How to Read Your First Free Book Online: A Step by Step Guide
description: You want to read a book online for free and you have no idea where to start. Here is exactly what to do, from search to reading.
content:
A friend recently asked me how to read a free book online. She had heard about Project Gutenberg but did not know how to use it. She tried once, found the website confusing, and gave up.

Her experience is common. Most free book sites were built by volunteers, not designers. The interfaces are plain, the navigation is inconsistent, and nothing guides you toward a good first book.

Here is a step by step guide that assumes you know nothing about ebooks and have never read one before.

## Step 1: Pick a Book You Already Know

Do not browse randomly. Pick a book you have heard of and have always meant to read. Pride and Prejudice, Alice in Wonderland, Frankenstein, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes. All of these are free.

## Step 2: Find It on BitLibrary

Open BitLibrary in your browser. Type the title into the search bar. Press Enter. Click the book when it appears in the results.

## Step 3: Start Reading

On the book's detail page, you will see a Read Online button. Click it. The book opens in your browser. You can scroll through pages, jump to chapters, and adjust the font size if the text is too small.

## Step 4: Set Up Your Reading Environment

| Setting | What to Change |
|---------|---------------|
| Font size | Increase it. Most screens need larger text than printed books. |
| Background | Switch to sepia or dark mode. White backgrounds cause eye strain. |
| Brightness | Lower it. You do not need full brightness for reading text. |
| Notifications | Turn them off. Even a quick glance breaks concentration. |

## Step 5: Read in Short Sessions

Do not try to read for an hour on your first try. Read for five minutes. Then ten. Build the habit slowly. Digital reading is a skill, and it takes time to get comfortable with it.

## What to Do When You Finish

Go back to the search bar. Pick another book. BitLibrary has thousands of them, all free, all available immediately. There is no limit on how many you can read.

If you prefer listening, most of the same books are available as audiobooks too. Press Play instead of Read, and let someone read to you.

title: Where to Start with Nepali Literature: A Beginner's Guide
description: Nepali literature can feel overwhelming. Here are the authors and books that make a good starting point, with recommendations for every taste.
content:
A friend once told me she wanted to read Nepali literature but did not know where to start. She had heard of Devkota and Parijat but had no sense of which books to pick first. She tried reading Muna Madan and found the language difficult. She put it down and did not try again for two years.

I made the same mistake. I started with the hardest book first and assumed if I could not get through it, Nepali literature was not for me.

It was for me. I just needed a better entry point.

## Start Here: The Most Accessible Books

| Book | Author | Why Start Here |
|------|--------|----------------|
| Palpasa Cafe | Narayan Wagle | A novel about the civil war, written in direct, modern Nepali. Reads fast. |
| Seto Dharti | Amar Neupane | A war story with clear characters and a gripping plot. No archaic language. |
| Sirishko Phool | Parijat | Short, intense, and deeply emotional. The language is poetic but not impenetrable. |
| Card Game | Indra Bahadur Rai | A collection of short stories in Nepali about daily life. Perfect for building confidence. |

These books were all published after 1960. Their language is closer to how Nepalis actually speak today. Save the classics for later.

## The Classics to Work Up To

Once you have read a few modern novels, the classics become easier.

| Book | Author | Why It Matters |
|------|--------|----------------|
| Muna Madan | Laxmi Prasad Devkota | The most beloved poem in Nepali. A short narrative about love and sacrifice. |
| Ghumne Mech Mathi Andho Manchhe | Bhupi Sherchan | A poetry collection that captures post-1950 Nepal with sharpness and wit. |
| Aamako Sapana | Gopal Prasad Rimal | A revolutionary poem that inspired a generation. Short enough to read in one sitting. |
| Sumnima | Mohan Koirala | A novel that blends myth and modernity. A milestone in Nepali fiction. |

## Where to Find These Books

Many of the modern titles are still under copyright. They are not available for free on BitLibrary, but you can find them in bookstores, libraries, and online retailers.

The classics are another story. Devkota's works, Sherchan's collections, and many pre-1970 texts are in the public domain. You can read them for free on BitLibrary.

For the modern works, the Research section on BitLibrary can help you find academic papers, reviews, and author interviews to learn more.
